examples.title: A full tank, then a stall
examples.situation: A cultivator sputters and dies; its fuel tank is full. The source answer says 'check air filter next.'
reasoning: Stop and make the machine safe. A full tank does not verify the fuel valve, switch, fuel feed or ignition.
A dirty/poorly seated air cleaner is one plausible cause and may be checked safely under the matched procedure; it is not an invariant first action.
Use the actual manual's chart, record findings and refer unsafe or unresolved work.
examples.takeaway: Investigate conditionally, with air-cleaner condition included; do not replace the plug or run the machine as a guess.

examples.title: Weeds remain but the engine is normal
examples.situation: After a permitted pass, weeds remain rooted and soil is wet; tine wear is unknown.
reasoning: Do not treat a poor result as proof of an engine fault.
Stop and assess soil timing, pass pace/setting and visible tine condition without touching moving parts.
Document crop condition, photo/observation and trainer decision before repeating any pass.
examples.takeaway: Several causes remain possible; adjust only under the trainer and manual, and refer damaged tines.

examples.title: Vibration rises suddenly
examples.situation: During a pass, vibration is much stronger than normal. The source offers loose bolts or damaged blades as possibilities.
reasoning: Stop immediately and keep people clear; do not feel the machine's live rotary or keep driving.
Once isolated/cooled, a qualified person checks permissible external fasteners and tines; engine/drive issues go to the technician.
Never create a loose-bolt fault on a machine to make this exercise realistic.
examples.takeaway: Report a hazardous stop and defer restart until the cause and repair are verified.

examples.title: Service log versus memory
examples.situation: A record says 'greased this week, filter washed, machine good' but gives no model, hour reading or element type.
reasoning: Identify actual model/manual, operating-hours record and its method, task date, observer and element type. Use a meter reading only if the actual machine has a meter.
Do not claim weekly grease for the SER or wash its paper element; assign the maker's scheduled/dealer work.
Record abnormal findings and whether practical actions were actually observed.
examples.takeaway: An auditable log with due work and honest status, not a blanket 'good' rating.
